vignette:
Karim

Karim is a 38-year-old Lebanese-born man who has worked as a hairdresser for nearly fifteen years, first in Beirut and then, after immigrating in his mid-twenties, in a busy salon in the city's west end. He is known among his clients as warm and talkative — the kind of stylist people book not just for a haircut but for the conversation. He has built his life carefully, chair by chair, client by client. That life felt solid to him until three years ago, when it came apart without warning.

It began with fatigue he dismissed as overwork. Then came the bruising — strange purple blooms appearing on his forearms without any injury he could account for. By the time he finally saw a doctor, his blood counts were alarming enough to send him directly to hospital. Within a week he had a diagnosis: acute myeloid leukemia. He was 35 years old and, as far as he had known that morning, perfectly healthy.

What followed was eight months of aggressive chemotherapy, a bone marrow transplant, and a prolonged hospitalization that he describes as feeling like being buried alive. He remembers the particular sound of the IV pump at three in the morning, the way the overhead light in his room never fully dimmed, the afternoon a nurse came in with a look on her face before she had said a word and he understood, in his body before his mind, that something had gone wrong. There was a period of septic shock during which he was told, later, that he had been close to dying. He has no memory of those four days, and the gap frightens him almost more than what he does remember.

He went into remission. People called it a miracle. His mother flew from Beirut and wept at his bedside. Friends brought food and flowers. Karim smiled and thanked everyone, and felt, beneath all of it, profoundly alone in something he could not name.

Now, two years out of treatment, he is back at the salon. His hair has grown back — thicker than before, he jokes, though the joke costs him something. He stands behind the chair for eight hours a day, running his hands through other people's hair, and he is good at it. But his mind does not stay in the room with him. Several times a week, without any clear trigger, he is pulled back into the hospital — the smell of the antiseptic, the cold weight of the IV line in his arm, the specific terror of not knowing if his body would survive the very treatment meant to save it. These moments arrive without warning and leave him short of breath, his heart loud in his chest, his hands continuing their work almost independently while some part of him is somewhere else entirely.

He sleeps poorly. He wakes between two and four in the morning and lies in the dark cataloguing sensations in his body — a twinge in his side, a headache, a patch of skin that feels different — convinced, again and again, that the cancer has returned. He has had scans that show nothing. The reassurance lasts perhaps a day. He has stopped telling people about this because he can see in their faces that they believe he should be grateful, and he is grateful, and neither of those things touches the fear.

He avoids the oncology ward where he was treated, rerouting his commute so he does not pass the hospital. He has declined two invitations to a cancer survivors' group. He tells himself he is busy.

What he finds hardest to explain — to his mother on the phone, to the few friends who ask — is that surviving did not feel like an ending. It felt like the moment the ground shifted, and he has not found his footing since. He cuts hair, he laughs with clients, he closes the salon at night. And he carries, quietly and alone, the knowledge of how quickly a body can become a place you are no longer safe inside.
